title: Developing and Validating the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Concept Inventory: an Instrument to Assess Artificial Intelligence Literacy among Middle School Students
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of reliable and valid instruments for assessing K-12 students’ artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, especially at the middle school level. The authors argue that without a general assessment tool, educators and researchers cannot clearly determine what AI concepts students can learn or how effective different AI literacy curricula and pedagogies are. To fill this gap, they developed the AI Literacy Concept Inventory (AI-CI), a multiple-choice assessment intended to measure middle school students’ conceptual understanding of core AI literacy topics.

The study combines qualitative and quantitative methods to design, refine, and validate the instrument. Qualitative work included expert panel reviews, observations of students in a pilot of the Developing AI Literacy (DAILy) curriculum, student interviews about their thinking, and cognitive validation interviews to identify misconceptions and improve item wording and distractors. Quantitative validation used responses from 981 middle school students across three U.S. public school districts, with a separate reliability sample of 108 students who took the AI-CI before and after learning with the DAILy curriculum. The assessment focused on AI general concepts, logic systems, machine learning, and supervised learning, and items were designed to be age-appropriate and technology-independent.

The authors conclude that the AI-CI is a valid and reliable tool for assessing AI literacy among middle school students. They also show that concept-inventory design can surface student misconceptions and provide more diagnostic information than standard multiple-choice tests, making the tool useful for both research and classroom assessment. Although the paper is not about teacher-facing generative AI tools, it is relevant to broader K-12 AI education because it clarifies how student learning of AI concepts can be measured and how misconceptions can be used to design better assessments.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / AI literacy context rather than a specific commercial product; in this paper it is discussed conceptually as AI systems that can generate content and as a topic in student AI literacy.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate a teacher-facing generative AI tool. It develops and validates an assessment of middle school students’ AI literacy, including concepts such as AI general, logic systems, machine learning, supervised learning, and mentions generative AI only as a concept students should understand.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical validation study, but it does not evaluate an AI instructional tool or intervention. The main contribution is assessment development/validation, so evidence is indirect for AI tool effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s impact is methodological rather than tool-intervention impact. It provides a validated assessment that could support future AI education studies, but it does not report outcome effects of an AI tool.
